The record describes special-category data under Article 9 — for example, health, biometric, or genetic data, or data revealing racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religious belief, or trade-union membership — data relating to criminal convictions or offences under Article 10, or other data whose sensitivity or personal nature creates a heightened risk to people's rights and freedoms, such as financial data revealing someone's economic situation or location data revealing their movements. The Article 29 Working Party's guidance (WP248, endorsed by the EDPB) names "sensitive data or data of a highly personal nature" as one of the criteria that triggers the Article 35 DPIA obligation — its own examples are a general hospital's patient records and a private investigator's file on offenders — and extends that same reasoning "beyond these provisions of the GDPR" to other categories the GDPR's own recitals treat as risk-increasing, including a person's financial circumstances and their location or movements. That guidance supports the assessment's position that a DPIA is required here. Section 1 records that determination. (Article 29 Working Party, Guidelines on Data Protection Impact Assessment (WP248 rev.01), Annex 1, criterion 4, adopted 4 October 2017; EDPB guidelines — interpretive guidance, not binding law, endorsed by the EDPB 25 May 2018.)
